description: "How the ZX Spectrum Next adds its sound sources into one stereo sum: the five inputs and their bits, why the sum never goes below its silent level of 1,536, how much of the range real music uses, the 12 bits the audio jack takes and what happens past them, the one-bit converters behind the jack and the speaker, HDMI's 48,000 samples a second, and how Klive's mixer keeps the same proportions."

import { Callout } from 'nextra/components'

# The Mixer: One Sum, Three Outputs

Every sound source on the Next adds its number to one sum, 28 million times a second. Nothing is ever
subtracted, so silence is not zero. And that one sum has to come out of a 3.5 mm jack, a small speaker
inside the case and an HDMI cable, all at the same time. How does a single number become three different
outputs, and how much room is there in it before the sound breaks?

This is the one place every program's sound passes through. A game's music, its effects, its sampled
speech and the beeper's clicks all meet here, and whether they come out clean depends on how they fit
together. A mix that is too loud does not merely get louder: it can break up. Know how the sum is built,
and you know how loud each part of your mix may be, and why the speaker can click while the headphones
stay quiet.

Read [The Big Picture: Four Sources, One Mixer](/en/under-the-hood/emulator-internals/next-audio/overview/) first. It introduces
the four kinds of source and the mixer, and here we take the mixer apart in full. The background chapter
[How a Computer Makes Sound](/en/under-the-hood/emulator-internals/computer-sound/) explains the terms
used below: a sample, a DAC, a filter, sound from a single bit and mixing. And if you read only one
chapter after the overview, well, make it this one.

## The road ahead

We start with the sum itself: five inputs, each lined up at its own place in 13 bits, placed so that the
adder can never overflow. Then comes a small surprise, why a silent Next does not add up to zero but to
1,536, and why that is a good thing. The key idea sits in the section after it, Headroom: how much of the
range real music takes, and what the audio jack does with a sum it cannot hold, which is not what you
would expect. From there we follow the sum out of the machine three ways: through the jack's one-bit
converter, through the little speaker on the board, and through HDMI, the only one of the three that
samples. We end with how Klive mixes the same sources in the same proportions, and which of the three
outputs you hear.

<Callout type="info">
Levels are in the **units of the Next's mixer**: the sum of one side runs from 0 to 8,191, and every
level here is a number on that scale (EAR is 512, one AY channel at full volume 255). Each side is mixed
on its own; the numbers are for one side. Figures of the hardware's sum and outputs are worked out from
the hardware's rules, since a capture would show Klive's centred form of them; the figure of Klive's mix
is captured from the emulated machine.
</Callout>

## Five inputs, one sum

The mixer has two sides, and on each it adds **five inputs**. The beeper gives two of them, one per bit
of port `$FE`; each of the other three kinds of source gives one. The sum is taken again at every tick of
the **28 MHz master clock**, so a change in any input reaches the sum within a 28-millionth of a second.

The sum is a **13-bit** number, 0 to 8,191. Each input is a binary number too, and the mixer lines it up
at a fixed place in those 13 bits before adding. Where an input sits decides how much it can add:

{/* /fig:inputs */}
<figcaption>The five inputs as the bits of the sum they occupy. An input placed two bits up counts four times as much: that is how the DACs' side is multiplied by 4.</figcaption>
</figure>

- **EAR**, port `$FE` bit 4, is one bit placed at **bit 9 of the sum**: 512 while the port bit is 1, 0
  while it is 0.
- **MIC** is one bit at **bit 7**: 128 or 0. It is port `$FE` bit 3, combined with the tape input and the
  Pi's EAR bit (the [overview](/en/under-the-hood/emulator-internals/next-audio/overview/#the-beeper-ear-and-mic)
  explains the combination). EAR and MIC count 4 to 1, as the 48K's resistors weighted them.
- **The AY chips** arrive as one 12-bit number per side, the channels of all three chips on that side
  already added together: **0 to 2,295**. One channel at full volume is 255. The TurboSound chapter's
  [Where the channels go](/en/under-the-hood/emulator-internals/next-audio/turbosound/#where-the-channels-go)
  explains how the channels are spread over the sides; with all three chips in mono, each chip gives both
  sides up to 765, three times 255.
- **The DACs** arrive as one 9-bit number per side, the side's two 8-bit channels added (A + B on the
  left, C + D on the right), 0 to 510. Placed two bits up, it counts four times: **0 to 2,040**.
- **The Pi** arrives as a 10-bit sample per side, **0 to 1,023**, added as it is.

So, what is the most they can add? Every input at its largest gives 512 + 128 + 2,295 + 2,040 + 1,023 =
**5,998**. The sum's 13 bits reach 8,191, so the sum itself can never overflow: the adder needs no check,
and nothing is cut off. Notice how neat that is. Overflow is not handled; it simply cannot happen.

The weights are no accident either. They keep EAR and MIC at the 48K's 4 to 1, and they make one DAC
channel's full swing, 255 steps of 4, a little louder than all three channels of one AY chip together
(1,020 against 765). That leaves room for drums and speech over AY music, which is what the Spectrum's DAC
sound cards were for.

## Silence is 1,536

Every input is a count upwards from zero. None of them can be negative, and the mixer never subtracts. A
sound is a movement **up and down around some level**, and here that level is whatever the sources add
while they are quiet.

That level is not zero, because two of the sources **rest in the middle** of their range:

- A **DAC** channel rests at `$80`, 128, halfway up its 0–255 range. A sample is a movement around that
  middle, so it has room to swing both ways. The two channels of a side add 256, which counts four times:
  **1,024**.
- The **Pi** rests at 512, the middle of its 0–1,023, for the same reason.
- The **AY chips** and the **beeper** rest at 0: an AY channel at volume 0, and EAR and MIC low.

So a silent Next adds **1,536** on each side, and stays there however long nothing plays.

Why go to the trouble? Because of the moment a source is switched on. If the DACs rested at 0 and jumped
to their middle when your program enabled them, the sum would leap by 1,024 in an instant, and the
speaker would answer with a loud **click**. The Next avoids that by holding them at `$80` **even while
they are switched off**. Bit 3 of the Peripheral 3 Setting register, NextReg `$08`, enables the DACs, and
while it is 0 every channel is held at `$80`, so switching them on or off changes nothing you can hear.
The Pi does the same: switched off or muted, it adds its resting 512, not 0. The beeper cannot play this
trick. The first time a program sets port `$FE` bit 4, the sum rises by 512, which is exactly the click a
48K made too.

Hey, and what happens to the constant 1,536? It is not lost on its way out, but you never hear it. After
the converters, outside the FPGA, the jack's circuit lets only changes through, as the background chapter
describes for
[a capacitor](/en/under-the-hood/emulator-internals/computer-sound/#several-sounds-at-once-are-added-together);
what reaches your headphones is the sound moving around zero.

## Headroom

How much of the range do real mixes use? Here are six of them, as the Next's hardware adds them: on the
sum's 0 to 8,191 scale, with a line at 4,095, which matters for the jack. They are worked out from the
mixer's rules, not captured; Klive's own range, which is counted differently, is in
[How Klive does it](#how-klive-does-it).

<figcaption>Six mixes on the hardware's sum, drawn to scale. Grey is the silent level; the coloured parts are the sources on top of it. Past the red line, the audio jack can no longer play the sum as it is.</figcaption>
</figure>

Let's work them out, for the left side:

1. **Silence**: the DACs at rest, 1,024, and the Pi at rest, 512: **1,536**.
2. **A 128K tune on one chip**, all three channels at full volume: on the left, channels A and B arrive
   (the TurboSound chapter's
   [Where the channels go](/en/under-the-hood/emulator-internals/next-audio/turbosound/#where-the-channels-go)),
   2 × 255 = 510: **2,046**.
3. **TurboSound**, nine channels at full volume: three chips' 510 each, 1,530: **3,066**.
4. **The same, with the beeper on top**, EAR and MIC both high, 640: **3,706**.
5. **Three chips in mono** at full volume, each giving 765 to both sides, 2,295, with EAR on top:
   **4,343**.
6. **Every source at its largest**, the DACs and the Pi at full scale instead of resting: **5,998**.

The sum handles all six: it has room up to 8,191. **The audio jack does not.** Its converters take only
the **lowest 12 bits** of the sum, 0 to 4,095, and leave bit 12 out. A sum below 4,096 arrives whole. A
sum of 4,096 or more loses its top bit, which takes 4,096 off it: 4,343 arrives as 247. Uhm, yes, you read
that right. The sound does not stop at a ceiling, as the background chapter's
[clipping](/en/under-the-hood/emulator-internals/computer-sound/#several-sounds-at-once-are-added-together)
would; it **wraps around** to the bottom of the range:

<figure>
{/* fig:wrap */}
<svg viewBox="0 0 700 306" role="img" aria-label="Two milliseconds of a loud 1,000 Hz tone whose sum swings from 1,300 to 4,700, drawn as a dashed curve, with a line at 4,095. The jack takes only the lowest 12 bits of the sum, so wherever the sum passes 4,095 the jack's value drops by 4,096 and starts again near zero: the solid curve follows the sum until it reaches the line, then falls to the bottom of the range, climbs, and jumps back up when the sum comes down again." style={{ width: "100%", height: "auto" }}>

<figcaption>A tone too loud for the jack. Each time the sum passes 4,095, the jack's value falls by 4,096, and the smooth wave becomes a series of jumps: a hard crackle, much harsher than a flattened top.</figcaption>
</figure>

Before you start to worry: in practice the jack has **2,559** units of room above silence, and it plays
everything a 128K tune or TurboSound in stereo can produce, with the beeper on top. What goes past is the
extreme: three chips in mono at full volume with the beeper, or a DAC or Pi sample near full scale on top
of loud music. So here is my advice: keep your total below 4,096, and you have nothing to worry about.
HDMI, which carries all 13 bits (see HDMI audio below), never wraps at all.

## The audio jack: one pin, 4,096 levels

The jack's sound leaves the FPGA as **one pin per side** that can only be on or off. Making 4,096
different levels from it is the job of a **one-bit converter**, the delta-sigma kind the background chapter
describes under
[sound from a single bit](/en/under-the-hood/emulator-internals/computer-sound/#sound-from-a-single-bit).

It works on the 28 MHz clock, one decision per tick:

1. The converter keeps a running total. At every tick it adds the input, the 12-bit value from the sum.
2. If the total is in the top half of its own range, the pin is **on** for this tick, and 4,096 is taken
   off the total. Otherwise the pin is **off**.
3. Over many ticks, the pin is on for exactly the share of ticks that the input is of 4,096. An input of
   1,024 switches it on one tick in four; 1,536, three ticks in eight.

<figure>
{/* fig:converter */}

The share of clocks the pin is on is the value divided by 4,096, and the resistor and capacitor after the pin turn that share into a voltage." style={{ width: "100%", height: "auto" }}>

<figcaption>The jack's converter for three inputs, 48 ticks each, computed exactly as the converter works. The pattern of on and off ticks repeats, and its average, dashed, is the input divided by 4,096.</figcaption>

The pin's pulses are far too fast to hear: the pattern repeats every few ticks, millions of times a
second. A **resistor and a capacitor** on the board after the pin, a low-pass filter, average them into a
smooth voltage: the larger the input, the higher the voltage. Then the circuit that removes the constant
level (see Silence is 1,536) leaves the sound alone for your headphones or amplifier.

Two things follow from this design, and I like both of them. The jack has **no sample rate**: its
converter follows the sum as it changes, at 28 MHz, so nothing is ever sampled and nothing is aliased on
the way out. And its resolution is the whole 12 bits: a change of a single unit in the sum moves the share
of on-ticks by one in 4,096.

## The internal speaker

The Next has a small speaker of its own on the board, driven by one more one-bit converter of the same
kind. It has no left and right, so it gets a **mono mix**: the left and right values the jack takes, both
12 bits, added together. Some boards bias the result to suit the transistor that drives the speaker, but
the idea is the same on all of them.

Two registers control it:

- The **Peripheral 3 Setting register, NextReg `$08`**, bit 4 switches the speaker **on** (1, the
  power-on value) or off. Off, the converter keeps running but its pin is held low.
- The **Peripheral 2 Setting register, NextReg `$06`**, bit 6 makes the speaker play **the beeper only**.
  With it set and the speaker on, EAR and MIC leave the mix of the jack and HDMI altogether, and the
  speaker gets a word of its own with nothing in it but them.

Here is what each output takes from the sum, bit by bit:

{/* /fig:bits */}
<figcaption>How the outputs take the 13-bit sum. The jack drops bit 12; HDMI sends all 13 bits inside a 16-bit word; the speaker, when it plays only the beeper, gets EAR and MIC alone.</figcaption>
</figure>

In the beeper-only word, EAR is bit 10 and MIC bit 8: 1,024 and 256 of the speaker's 8,191, the same
4-to-1 ratio, and as loud as EAR and MIC are in the speaker's normal mix, where each side brings its 512
and 128. What is that mode for? A program that wants its key clicks and alerts to stay in the machine
while its music goes to the headphones. Mind one thing, though: the beeper's sound is moved, not copied,
so the headphones no longer hear it.

## HDMI audio

HDMI carries the picture as numbers, and its sound as numbers too: **48,000 samples a second** for each
side, travelling between the lines of the picture. The Next builds each sample as a **16-bit word**: a 0,
the whole 13-bit sum, and two 0 bits at the bottom (the figure in the previous section). The word is
therefore the sum times 4, and it never wraps: 5,998 arrives as 23,992.

The **Peripheral 4 Setting register, NextReg `$09`**, bit 2 silences HDMI audio, for a television whose
own speakers should stay quiet while the sound goes through the jack.

Unlike the jack, HDMI **samples** the sum. 48,000 times a second it takes the sum's value at that moment,
without averaging what happened since the last one. A change that falls between two samples is seen only
at the next one, up to a 48,000th of a second (21 µs) late:

<figure>
{/* fig:hdmi */}
<svg viewBox="0 0 700 284" role="img" aria-label="0.6 milliseconds of a beeper square wave of 6,875 Hz in the sum, drawn as a thin line whose edges fall anywhere in time. The dots are the moments HDMI takes the sum's value, 48,000 times a second, and the thick staircase is what HDMI sends: each edge moves to the next dot, so the steps are three or four samples long, not the even three and a half of the real wave." style={{ width: "100%", height: "auto" }}>

<figcaption>A fast beeper tone and what HDMI makes of it, worked out from the sampling rule. Every edge moves to the next sample, so the steps come out three or four samples long instead of an even three and a half.</figcaption>
</figure>

Should you care? For most sound, no: 48,000 samples a second is enough for anything a human hears, as the
background chapter explains under
[Fast enough](/en/under-the-hood/emulator-internals/computer-sound/#fast-enough-or-it-sounds-wrong).
For the sharp edges of the beeper it is a small cost: an edge that moves by up to one sample adds a faint
roughness, a little aliasing, to a high beeper tone that the jack plays clean. [The last chapter](/en/under-the-hood/emulator-internals/next-audio/klive-audio/#a-moment-or-a-window) shows the same
choice in an emulator, which must sample too.

The constant level travels with the numbers: a silent Next sends 1,536 × 4 = 6,144 in every word.

## How Klive does it

Klive makes **one** stream of samples, at the rate the IDE's audio runs at (48,000 a second by default),
and hands it to your computer's sound card. Your computer has one pair of speakers, so that stream plays
**one** of the Next's outputs: the one chosen under **Machine › Sound › Output** (also in **Settings ›
Emulator**), the audio jack unless you choose otherwise.

The hardware's sum is a number inside the FPGA; what reaches your headphones is that sum after the
converter and the circuit that removes its constant level. Klive's samples stand for that later point,
**the sound after the capacitor**, which is why they move around zero.

Each time it needs a sample, Klive's mixer asks every source for its level at that moment and adds them
in the hardware's units, with three changes that play the capacitor's part:

- The **DACs and the Pi** are counted from their resting levels: a DAC channel at `$80` and the Pi at 512
  add 0. Silence is 0 instead of 1,536.
- The **beeper's** EAR and MIC pass through a filter that removes their constant level slowly (a constant
  falls to about a third in a little over a tenth of a second), as the capacitor after the jack's
  converters does. A beeper wave ends up moving around zero.
- The **AY chips** are added as they are, from 0 upwards.

The sum is then multiplied by **12.8** and becomes a signed 16-bit sample, −32,768 to 32,767. Here is the
beeper switched on from silence, as the hardware sums it inside the FPGA and as Klive mixes it:

<figcaption>The beeper switched on from silence, at two points of the chain. Top, the hardware's digital sum inside the FPGA, worked out from the rules: 1,536 and 2,048, all of it above zero. Bottom, Klive's mix, captured from the emulated machine, which stands for the sound after the jack's capacitor: the same 512-unit square, sliding down to centre on zero within about a tenth of a second. The real jack's output slides to zero in the same way.</figcaption>
</figure>

So the two traces do not disagree: they show the sound before and after the capacitor, and Klive's is the
one you hear. The constant level and its slow drift are far below any pitch. A waveform drawn from Klive's
samples sits around zero, which is why the captures in these sound chapters are drawn about their middle
level.

Why 12.8? Because it gives Klive **the jack's headroom**. The jack plays the sum cleanly up to 4,095, which
is 2,559 above the silent 1,536; Klive maps 2,559 units to 2,559 × 12.8 = 32,755, just inside its largest
sample. So **every mix the jack plays cleanly, Klive plays without loss**, nine AY channels at full volume
and the beeper included.

Each of the **three outputs** is played as the hardware builds it, from the same sum:

- **Audio jack**: the sum's lowest 12 bits. A mix past 4,095 **wraps around** as it does on the real
  jack (see Headroom): Klive works out the hardware's sum beside its own mix, and takes 4,096 off its
  sample each time the sum passed 4,096. Below the limit, the jack's sample is exactly the mix described
  above.
- **Internal speaker**: the left and right jack values added into one mono mix, on both sides of the
  stream, multiplied by 6.4 (the speaker's room above its silent 3,072 is twice the jack's). NextReg
  `$08` bit 4 off silences it. With NextReg `$06` bit 6 set, it plays only the beeper, EAR at 1,024 and
  MIC at 256: as loud as the beeper is on the jack, which then no longer carries it. Klive follows the
  later boards' speaker; the earliest boards bias the speaker's word for their transistor.
- **HDMI**: the whole sum, never wrapping, multiplied by 7.34 so that even every source at its largest
  (4,462 above silence) fits. Like the hardware, it takes the sum's value at each sample's moment: the
  beeper's level and the AY chips' output at that instant, not their average since the last sample.
  NextReg `$09` bit 2 silences it.

The choice belongs to Klive, not to the machine: it survives a reset, and switching it never restarts the
machine.

Klive's tape deck feeds the Next's EAR socket: its level passes the machine's own input stage (the
debounce that drops pulses under about 1.14 µs, the relaxation that turns a level held at 1 into 0 after
about 1.15 ms), and the result reaches port `$FE` bit 6 and the MIC line, so a loading tape is heard at
MIC's level as on the real machine. What **Klive leaves out** are three small differences that come from
its way of removing the constant level. None of them can be heard, since a constant level never is:

- **Only the beeper is filtered.** The real capacitor removes the constant level of the whole sum. Klive
  filters the beeper and counts the DACs and the Pi from their fixed resting levels, but leaves the AY
  chips as they are: an AY channel held at a fixed volume stays in Klive's samples as a steady offset,
  where the real circuit would let it fade to zero. Filtering the whole sum instead would cost room: a
  sudden step passes a filter at full size, so the samples would reach Klive's limit sooner.
- **How fast the constant level fades.** Klive's filter is tuned to about a tenth of a second; the values
  of the real board's resistor and capacitor are not part of the machine's design, so the real jack may
  fade faster or slower.
- **HDMI's constant level.** The Next's HDMI samples carry the silent level, 1,536 × 4 = 6,144 in every
  word; Klive's HDMI output is centred on zero like its other outputs.

And if you want to read the code yourself, here is where it lives:

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| The sum, the resting levels, the beeper's filter, the factors and the limit | `src/emu/machines/zxNext/wasm/zxnext/zxnext-audio-mixer.c` |
| The three outputs, the jack's wrap and the beeper-only switch | the same file |
| The sound output setting | `src/common/settings/next-audio-output.ts` |
| Each source's level | `zxnext-beeper.c`, `zxnext-psg.c`, `zxnext-dac.c`, `zxnext-pi-i2s.c` in the same folder |
| The tape deck and the EAR input stage | `zxnext-tape.c` in the same folder |

## What to take home

Let's put the sum back together. On each side, the Next's mixer adds **five inputs** at 28 MHz, each lined up at its
own place in a 13-bit sum: EAR at bit 9 (512), MIC at bit 7 (128), the AY chips (0 to 2,295), the DACs
(0 to 510, counted four times, so 0 to 2,040) and the Pi (0 to 1,023). Every input at its largest gives
**5,998**, inside the sum's **8,191**, so the sum never overflows.

Every input counts up from zero, and the DACs and the Pi rest in the middle of their range, `$80` and 512,
even while they are switched off: a silent Next sums to **1,536**, and switching those sources never
clicks. The circuit after the converters removes that constant level before you hear anything.

The **audio jack** takes only the sum's lowest **12 bits**, up to 4,095, which leaves 2,559 above
silence: enough for nine AY channels at full volume and the beeper. Past 4,095 the jack's value **wraps
around**, a hard crackle rather than a flattened top. Its **one-bit converter** switches a pin on for the
input's share of 4,096 of the 28 MHz ticks, a resistor and capacitor smooth that into a voltage, and so
the jack has no sample rate at all. The **internal speaker** plays the left and right values added,
through one more such converter; NextReg `$08` bit 4 switches it on, and NextReg `$06` bit 6 gives it the
beeper alone, which then leaves the jack and HDMI. **HDMI** sends the whole sum as 16-bit words, 48,000 a
second, taking the sum's value at each sample's moment; NextReg `$09` bit 2 silences it.

Klive mixes in the same units, counts the DACs and the Pi from their resting levels, filters the beeper's
constant level away and multiplies by **12.8**, so its range matches the jack's. It plays the **output you
choose**, the jack with its wrap, the speaker or HDMI, each built as on the hardware. Keep your mix under
